=== Final DCC Comments on Demand Management Service (Project 58482).pdf ===
                                             PROJECT NO. 58482

 RULEMAKING TO DEVELOP A                              §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 RELIABILITY SERVICE TO                               §
 COMPETITIVELY PROCURE DEMAND                         §
 REDUCTIONS FROM LARGE LOADS                          §
 UNDER PURA §39.170                                   §                    OF TEXAS


                         COMMENTS OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

                                             I.​   INTRODUCTION

        DCC is the national membership association for the data center industry, representing leading

data center owners and operators who maintain data center infrastructure across the country and globe, as

well as companies that lease large amounts of data center capacity. DCC empowers and champions the

data center community through public policy advocacy, thought leadership, stakeholder outreach, and

community engagement. As the voice of the data center industry, DCC also advocates for a highly skilled

and diverse technology workforce, and a competitive business environment to support the growth and

success of this essential business sector.

        Texas has emerged as a premier data center market, fueled by significant investment, resilient

infrastructure, and a highly skilled workforce. A vast majority of DCC members have teams, operations

and infrastructure in the Lone Star State, and 11 companies are proudly headquartered within its borders.

Texas's commitment to grid reliability, combined with a business-friendly environment, makes the state an

attractive destination for continued investment.

        As electricity demand continues to grow, DCC is committed to working collaboratively with the

Commission, utilities, and other stakeholders on solutions that continue to support the integration of new

large load customers while advancing an affordable and reliable grid for all Texans.



                      II.​   RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF QUESTIONS

        The Data Center Coalition (DCC) appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments to the

Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) regarding Project No. 58482, Rulemaking to Develop a
 Reliability Service to Competitively Procure Demand Reductions from Large Loads Under PURA

§39.170. DCC commends the Commission for seeking input from industry stakeholders on this

rulemaking proposal.



        Question 1: Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a

        seasonal service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?



        As the Commission develops the reliability service program to implement PURA § 39.170(b), the

overarching objective should be to ensure that ERCOT and participating customers have sufficient

advance clarity, predictability, and operational certainty to respond effectively to reliability events.

Although extreme weather and system conditions cannot always be forecasted with precision, the

reliability service—regardless of whether it is structured as an as‑needed or seasonal program—should

include clearly defined parameters that enable ERCOT to engage in advance planning and allow

participating loads to understand their potential obligations. Large load customers, in particular, require

adequate notice and transparent program rules to safely and reliably plan for potential curtailments,

including adjustments to operations, staffing, and contractual commitments. Accordingly, the

Commission should prioritize program design principles that:

    ●​ Provide sufficient advance notice of enrollment requirements, availability expectations, and

        potential activation conditions; and

    ●​ Enable participating customers to reasonably anticipate when demand reductions may be

        requested and to prepare to respond in a timely and effective manner.

        Ultimately, the effectiveness of the reliability service program in procuring meaningful and

dependable demand reductions will depend on the extent to which the program ensures that participants

can know, plan, and respond when called upon to support system reliability.
         Question 2: PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a

        reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA

        § 39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods when the

        service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.

                a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances other

        than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

                b. Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how should it

        be defined?



        DCC interprets PURA §39.170(b) as authorizing deployment of the reliability service solely in

response to extreme weather events. The statute directs the Commission to require ERCOT to develop a

reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition, and §39.170(b)(1)

further specifies that the rules governing the service must identify the periods when it may be used to

assist with maintaining reliability specifically “during extreme weather events.” The Legislature’s intent

appears to be developing the service as a weather-related emergency tool.

        Further, the Commission should define "extreme weather event" in this rulemaking. A clear and

bounded definition is essential to ensuring that the service is deployed consistently and predictably, which

will support greater participation. The definition applied in this rulemaking should remain consistent with

previous definitions of extreme weather events supported by the Commission, such as the criteria

proposed in PURA §25.483(j)(1), which provides clear, measurable parameters.



        Question 3: PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit

        participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price of

        electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a different reliability

        or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)-which allows ERCOT to direct a large load

        customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its backup
         generation under certain circumstances-states that a large load customer with onsite

        backup generation may participate in a service authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).

                 a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load

        customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

                 b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should

        apply to participation in the new service?

                 c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four

        coincident peaks (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new

        service?

                 d. Should the commission define "curtailment in response to wholesale price of

        electricity" and, if so, how should it be defined?



​       DCC believes that the qualification standard for demonstrating a 24 hour ramp down should be

both technology and customer specific. The operational processes required to safely curtail load vary

depending on the nature of a customer’s equipment and facility configuration. In some cases, there are a

number of manual steps that need to be taken to curtail without risk of damaging equipment or safety

incidents. As such, the Commission should offer flexibility in the rulemaking that accounts for variances

in operations.

        Additionally, we believe that only the prohibitions explicitly stated in the statute should be

applied. Imposing additional prohibitions not laid out in the language of Senate Bill 6 would risk

unnecessarily restricting the pool of eligible participants, reducing the program's effectiveness, and

exceeding the Commission's statutory authority. If the Commission identifies specific reliability or

operational concerns that it believes warrant additional eligibility restrictions, we request the opportunity

to comment on any such proposals before they are incorporated into a final rule.

​       Following this logic, we do not believe that participation in four coincident peaks (4CP) or any

successor transmission cost allocation methodology should preclude a customer from participating in the
 new reliability service. The 4CP methodology is a transmission cost allocation mechanism that

determines how certain transmission charges are distributed among customers based on their demand

during peak hours of the year. It is not a reliability service, an ancillary service, or a curtailment program.

These are fundamentally different economic and operational activities, and treating the 4CP participation

as a disqualifier for this demand response program would be inconsistent with the statute and would

unnecessarily exclude a significant segment of potential participants.



        Question 4: How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?



        DCC recommends that the Commission establish a framework in which target quantities are

determined based on ERCOT's seasonal reliability assessments and prices are established through a

competitive procurement process.

        Regarding quantities, ERCOT's seasonal reliability assessments provide the most technically

grounded and timely basis for determining how much capacity should be procured under this program.

Because these assessments are forward looking over a near-term period, they more accurately reflect grid

conditions than a fixed procurement target set far in advance. Tying target quantities to this existing

process would ensure procurement levels are aligned with actual reliability needs and avoid the risk of

overprocurement that comes with longer-range estimation.

        For price, DCC recommends that the Commission require ERCOT to procure this service through

a competitive market-based mechanism, consistent with ERCOT's existing market design principles.

Competitive procurement ensures that the price of this service reflects the actual value participants place

on their ability to curtail, which in turn will produce outcomes that are both economically and equitable

for participants. This approach is also more likely to attract a larger pool of participants over time,

strengthening the program's overall reliability benefit.
         Question 5: What additional information should the Commission consider in its

        implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)?



        Large load customers, such as data centers, site backup generators as an emergency resource to

ensure continuity of operations during grid outages. If large load customers leverage on-site diesel backup

generators for extended periods to provide reliability support, the Commission should consider the air

permitting regulations that pertain to them when crafting rules. These include compliance with state and

federal air permitting regulations, local ordinances (such as notice restrictions), industry sustainability

commitments, availability and transportation of fuel supply, price impacts, and costs associated with

operations and maintenance. If a company wants to participate in the demand response program, they may

face restrictions on the air emissions side. As previously noted, backup diesel generators are subject to

strict emissions limits under state and federal law that cap their annual usage.

        Large load customers should not face regulatory penalties for switching to backup generation in

response to emergency grid conditions. Therefore, interagency coordination is essential during requests

for reliability support. DCC recommends that a formal process be established through which ERCOT, the

Commission, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), and the Environmental

Protection Agency (EPA) coordinate to provide enforcement discretion. This would help ensure that large

loads remain compliant while helping support ERCOT in managing reliability events.



        Question 6: PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent

        organization certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that

        each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned

        utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the

        installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is

        interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric

        cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer
         with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner. This

        subsection applies only to a load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is not: (1)

        Load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2)

        Designated as a critical natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission

        include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA §39.170(a)?



        DCC believes that the Commission should take up PURA §39.170(a) as a separate rulemaking.

While related, the obligations established under this statute require distinct stakeholder consideration that

merit a separate, more focused conversation.

​       Despite this, DCC emphasizes the critical importance of the utility and customer collaboration

ahead of any load shed events and throughout. The statute's language directs TDSPs to "confer with the

customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner." This language reflects an

understanding that curtailment is not a one-size-fits-all process. To accommodate and prepare for this, it’s

critical that flushed out processes are established to ensure a smooth procurement of this service in the

midst of an emergency event. DCC also believes that the Commission should involve other necessary

entities, including TCEQ and other relevant stakeholders, to ensure all operational expectations and any

legal ramifications are identified and addressed upfront.

​       We further recommend that the Commission consider allowing customers to redirect load shed

events to other facilities in cases that are operationally practical. It is not uncommon for a large load

customer to operate multiple facilities, and one site may be better positioned to absorb curtailment while

still providing the reliability needed to the grid. Preserving this ability could be consistent with the statute

language that emphasizes that this be done in a “coordinated manner” that would improve the overall

effectiveness for all stakeholders during emergency situations.
                                          III.​   CONCLUSION

        Data centers are critical to our modern economy and daily lives, and our industry is eager to

contribute to solutions that ensure reliable, affordable and adequate power for all consumers. DCC is

committed to being a collaborative partner and a part of the solution to meeting Texas's energy demand

and reliability goals. We look forward to continued engagement with the Commission, utilities,

customers, and other stakeholders in Texas.



                                                         Respectfully submitted,

​                                                        Cameron Poursoltan
​                                                        Data Center Coalition
                                                         Cameron@datacentercoalition.org
